title: What a chart can tell me
text: A chart makes some patterns easier to see, but it also reflects a series of choices. Which observations belong in the plot? What belongs on each axis? Which differences deserve attention?

title: What a chart can tell me
text:
One choice that matters
In a comparison of income and life expectancy, a logarithmic income axis changes the spacing of the values. That can help reveal patterns that are difficult to see when a few large values stretch the scale.

title: What a chart can tell me
section: What I still need to ask
text:
What I still need to ask
A visible association does not explain why the pattern exists. Before moving from description to explanation, I need to think about the research question, the data, and possible alternative explanations.
My next step is to describe the plot in one careful sentence, then write down a question it cannot answer.

What I learned

Travel is most rewarding when you arrive with curiosity rather than expectations. The moments I remember most from Oxford were often the ones I never planned for.
Living and studying in another country taught me to pay closer attention to how history, culture, and daily life shape the way people think and communicate.
I learned that there is value in slowing down, observing, and asking questions. Understanding a place comes less from seeing famous landmarks and more from listening to the people who call it home.

When Words Become Risk: War Rhetoric and Safe-Haven Currency Markets
UNDERGRADUATE HONORS THESIS · IN PROGRESS
Question How does war threat rhetoric influence safe-haven currency markets?
Description This project examines the relationship between geopolitical rhetoric and foreign exchange markets. Rhetoric data are merged with CHF, JPY, and USD exchange-rate data obtained from FRED and benchmarked against the Caldara and Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk (GPR) Index. Regression analysis is used to estimate the effects of geopolitical rhetoric on exchange-rate returns, while GARCH models are employed to assess its impact on exchange-rate volatility.

title: How was Trump’s proposed border wall discussed in his 2019 tweets?
text:
Question
How did Donald Trump discuss the proposed U.S.–Mexico border wall in his 2019 tweets, and how did the sentiment and recurring themes of wall-related tweets compare with his broader Twitter communication?

Data
This project analyzes 4,469 tweets posted by Donald Trump between January 1 and December 31, 2019.
The dataset (trump_tweets_2019.csv) contains one tweet per observation. I included all tweets in the supplied 2019 corpus.
Tweets were classified as wall-related if their text contained at least one of the following terms or phrases: “wall,” “barrier,” “fence,” “border security,” “southern border,” “caravan,” or “shutdown.”

237 wall-related tweets (5.3%)
4,232 other tweets (94.7%)



Methods
Sentiment: I used the Bing Liu sentiment dictionary, which assigns positive words a value of +1 and negative words a value of −1. I summed matched word values within each tweet to calculate a net sentiment score, then averaged the scores across tweets in each group.


Word frequency
The most frequently used terms provide an overview of recurring language in Trump’s 2019 tweets.


Topics:
I used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to identify recurring themes across the 2019 corpus. Text was tokenized, converted to lemmas, and stripped of SMART stopwords and selected additional terms.
I selected four topics (k = 4) to distinguish recurring themes in Trump’s communication. The document-term matrix retained 4,441 tweets; 28 tweets with no retained words were excluded from topic modeling. I interpreted the topics by examining their most prominent keywords and original tweets.

title: How was Trump’s proposed border wall discussed in his 2019 tweets?
text:
Sentiment finding
Wall-related tweets had a mean net sentiment score of −0.203, compared with +0.277 for other tweets.
This indicates that wall-related tweets contained a more negative balance of dictionary words than Trump’s other 2019 tweets. However, dictionary scores measure word-level sentiment, not Trump’s overall position toward the border wall.
 Mean net Bing Liu sentiment score per tweet among Trump’s 2019 posts. Tweets were classified as wall-related based on keyword matches. Negative scores indicate more negative than positive matched words; they do not necessarily indicate opposition to the wall.

title: How was Trump’s proposed border wall discussed in his 2019 tweets?
text:
Topic finding
The LDA model identified four recurring themes:

Foreign Policy & National Interests
Partisan Politics & Elections
Border Security & Economic Promises
Media Criticism & Fake News

Wall-related tweets had a higher average proportion of the Border Security & Economic Promises topic (30.1%) than other tweets (24.6%). The other three topics were less represented in the wall-related group.

Average estimated topic proportions across modeled documents, comparing wall-related and other tweets. Each bar represents the mean proportion of a topic within the group’s document mixtures.*

title: How was Trump’s proposed border wall discussed in his 2019 tweets?
text:
Check the original texts
Sentiment example — Tweet 112

“The damage done to our Country from a badly broken Border - Drugs, Crime and so much that is bad - is far greater than a Shutdown…”

Tweet 112 received a net sentiment score of −5 because the dictionary identified five negative words: damage, badly, broken, crime, and bad. Yet Trump used this negative language to characterize border conditions and argue for addressing the situation.
This illustrates the difference between negative vocabulary and the overall political message of a tweet.
Topic example — Topic 1 One high-weight Topic 1 tweet discussed South Korea’s increased payments to the United States for its defense, while another discussed Trump’s trade negotiations with China’s President Xi.
These examples support the interpretation of Topic 1 as Foreign Policy & National Interests.

Limits
Sentiment: Dictionary-based analysis cannot reliably identify sarcasm, negation, context, or the target of a statement. As Tweet 112 illustrates, negative language can be used to support a political argument rather than express opposition to a policy. Dictionary coverage was also relatively low, meaning most words did not contribute to the scores.
Topics: LDA identifies patterns of word co-occurrence rather than objectively defined subjects. Tweets can address multiple themes, and topic labels require researcher interpretation. Results also depend on preprocessing decisions and the selected number of topics. The differences in average topic proportions are descriptive and were not tested for statistical significance.
The topic model identified four recurring themes in Trump’s 2019 Twitter communication: international trade and relations, partisan conflict, campaign messaging and border security, and media criticism. Border security appeared alongside electoral and political messaging, suggesting that discussion of the border was embedded within broader political communication rather than isolated to immigration policy.


Answer to the question
Trump’s wall-related tweets differed from his broader 2019 communication in both sentiment vocabulary and thematic emphasis. Wall-related tweets had a more negative average dictionary score, while topic modeling showed a greater emphasis on border security and economic promises.
Together, these findings suggest that Trump’s border-related messaging frequently framed the issue through negative descriptions of border conditions and arguments about security and economic interests. However, text analysis alone cannot establish Trump’s underlying intentions or how audiences interpreted his messages.
